Wolfgang Capito
VOLF-gang KAP-ih-toh
proper noun (figure)
German Wolfgang — from wolf (“wolf”) and gang (“path, going”). His surname is a Latinized form of the German Köpfel (“little head”), rendered as Capito after the Roman fashion by which Renaissance scholars dressed their names in Latin.

📖 Biblical Definition

Wolfgang Capito (1478–1541 AD) was a Hebraist, humanist, and Reformer of Strasbourg, and, with Martin Bucer, one of the two chief architects of the Reformation in that free imperial city. Trained in medicine, law, and theology, and reckoned among the ablest Hebrew scholars of his age, Capito served for a time in the household of Albert of Mainz, the very prelate whose indulgence-traffic Luther had assailed; yet the light of the recovered gospel drew him out of the shadow of Rome. By 1523 he had settled in Strasbourg, cast in his lot openly with the evangelical cause, and taken a lawful wife, testifying with his life against the unscriptural yoke of enforced clerical celibacy. There he laboured alongside Bucer to plant Reformed preaching, to order the churches, and to catechize the people in the pure doctrine of justification by faith alone. Capito was, by temperament, an irenic and conciliatory man, sometimes drawn too near to the Anabaptists and to compromise in his longing for concord; but the mature course of his ministry ran in the Reformed channel of Strasbourg, honoring the sole authority of Scripture and the free grace of God in Christ. He died of the plague in 1541, a faithful under-shepherd whose Hebrew learning and patient labour helped make Strasbourg a nursery of the Reformed faith and a refuge to the persecuted.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Hebraist and Reformer of Strasbourg (1478–1541 AD); with Bucer the chief planter of the Reformed church in that city.

WOLFGANG CAPITO, proper noun. German Wolfgang + Latinized Capito (from Köpfel, “little head”).

German Reformer and Hebrew scholar (1478–1541 AD); trained in medicine, law, and theology.

Colleague of Martin Bucer at Strasbourg; together they ordered the Reformed church of that free imperial city.

Formerly in the service of Albert of Mainz; drawn to the evangelical cause and married by 1523, forsaking enforced celibacy.

An irenic man, sometimes over-conciliatory toward Anabaptists; died of the plague in 1541.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of patient, learned labour joined to the pure gospel.

expand to see more

Capito is remembered, when he is remembered at all, chiefly as a lesser satellite of Bucer, and the temptation is to let his Hebrew learning and his quiet, irenic labour be swallowed up in the fame of his more forceful colleagues. That is a species of forgetfulness, not of falsification; the man himself taught no error worth naming as corruption, and his mature ministry ran soundly in the Reformed channel of Strasbourg.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What Capito recovers for us is the marriage of deep learning to a humble, peace-loving spirit poured out in the ordinary work of ordering a church and catechizing a people. His over-fondness for concord is a warning that peace must never be purchased at the price of doctrine; yet his patient scholarship and his willingness to labour in another man’s shadow rebuke our appetite for prominence and teach us to seek the good of Christ’s church rather than our own name.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

German Wolfgang + Latinized Capito; the Hebraist Reformer of Strasbourg, colleague of Bucer.
